section: Community section 12, "The Math of Absorption, and Who This Isn't For"
about: The words each preservation unit of STANCE-LEDGER-s12.md rests on (U7 corrected to "for community", Joel 2026-10-12 05:33; U29 and U30 from his answers 17b and his P16 sentence). Check: python3 tools/humanization/preservation_keys.py s12/preservation-keys.json DRAFT.

units.what: the article asks people to talk about all eight hard things
many intelligent adults would rather talk solar panels for hours
he understands why
modern life trains us to perform competence and hide
screens let us escape discomfort instantly
institutions reward narrow skills, then act surprised (both halves of the quip)
the question isn't whether someone is "good enough" for community
the practical question: attention for others, willingness to examine own reactions, whether the group has enough capacity without being consumed
units.note: 2026-10-12 17:23: Joel's P3 ("enough free resource/capacity", "without becoming a full-time caretaker operation") is his authorized wording.

units.what: practice, luck in childhood, surviving an emergency needing care more than responsibility; most of us move between
the community shares some therapist functions; peer counseling: listen, accompany, help process ordinary emotional material
that doesn't make the community infinitely absorbent
free resource, from Re-evaluation Counseling: attention, steadiness, skill, practical capacity after enough of one's own material
need is what currently requires support
everyone carries both; the ratio changes
his need exceeded his free resource many times; Good Lord
his story, every fact
he could go on; little left for anybody else
stabilize and do inner pl/ork before helping found a community; not from a mountaintop
a group can absorb only as much need as its members have free resource to meet
eight people with two in sustained crisis may spend most attention; eighty can often spread the same need
so welcoming is partly a resource question, not a measure of compassion
saying yes beyond capacity can hurt existing members and the newcomer
the paradox: small communities need members most and can absorb disruption least
